source_text: Conati sunt enim quidam persuadere deum patrem non esse omnipotentem; non quia hoc dicere ausi sunt, sed in suis traditionibus hoc sentire et credere conuincuntur. cum enim dicunt esse naturam, quam deus omnipotens non creauerit, de qua tamen istum mundum fabricauerit, quem pulchre ordinatum esse concedunt, ita omnipotentem deum negant, ut non eum credant mundum potuisse facere, nisi ad eum fabricandum alia natura, quae iam fuerat et quam ipse non fecerat, uteretur; carnali scilicet consuetudine uidendi fabros et domorum structores et quoslibet opifices, qui, nisi adiuuentur parata materia, ad effectum suae artis peruenire non possunt, ita intellegunt fabricatorem mundi non esse omnipotentem, si mundum fabricare non posset, nisi eum aliqua non ab illo fabricata natura tamquam materies adiuuaret. ac si omnipotentem deum fabricatorem mundi esse concedunt, fateantur necesse est ex nihilo eum fecisse quae fecit. non enim aliquid esse potest, cuius creator non esset, cum esset omnipotens, quia etsi aliquid fecit ex aliquo, sicut hominem de limo, non utique fecit ex eo, quod ipse non fecerat, quia terram, unde limus est, ex nihilo fecerat. et si ipsum caelum et terram, id est )mundum et omnia, quae in eo sunt, ex aliqua materia fecerat, sicut scriptum est: qui fecisti mundum ex materia inuisa, uel etiam informi, sicut nonnulla exemplaria tenent, nullo modo credendum est illam ipsam materiam, de qua factus est mundus, quamuis informem, quamuis inuisam, quocumque modo esset, per se ipsam esse potuisse tamquam coaeternam et coaeuam deo; sed quemlibet modum suum, quem habebat, ut quoquo modo esset et distinctarum rerum formas posset accipere, non habebat nisi ab omnipotente deo, cuius beneficio est res non solum quaecumque formata, sed etiam quaecumque formabilis. inter formatum autem et formabile hoc interest, quod formatum iam accepit formam, formabile autem potest accipere. sed qui praestat rebus formam, ipse praestat etiam posse formari, quoniam de illo et in illo est omnium speciosissima species incommutabilis, et ideo ipse unus est, qui cuilibet rei non solum, ut pulchra sit, sed etiam ut pulchra esse possit adtribuit. quapropter rectissime creditur omnia deum fecisse de nihilo: quia etiam si de aliqua materia factus est mundus, eadem ipsa materia de nihilo facta est, ut ordinatissimo dei munere prima capacitas formarum fieret, ac deinde formarentur quaecumque formata sunt. hoc autem diximus, ne quis existimet contrarias sibi esse diuinarum scripturarum sententias, quoniam et omnia deum de nihilo fecisse scriptum est et mundum esse factum de informi materia.
thought_title: God made all things from nothing
orientation: Augustine is beginning his exposition of the creed by defending the first article, that God the Father is almighty, against those who say he needed pre-existing matter to make the world.
pass_a_gloss: For some have tried to persuade that God the Father is not almighty; not because they have dared to say this, but in their own traditions they are convicted of thinking and believing this. For when they say that there is a nature, which almighty God did not create, from which nevertheless he built this world, which they admit is beautifully ordered, they deny that God is almighty in such a way that they do not believe that he could have made the world, unless for building it he used another nature, which already existed and which he himself had not made; clearly by the carnal habit of seeing craftsmen and builders of houses and any workmen, who, unless they are helped by prepared material, cannot arrive at the effect of their own art, they understand that the maker of the world is not almighty, if he could not build the world unless some nature not built by him helped him as material. And if they admit that almighty God is the maker of the world, they must necessarily confess that he made from nothing the things which he made. For nothing can exist whose creator he would not be, since he is almighty, because even if he made something from something, as man from mud, he certainly did not make it from that which he himself had not made, because the earth, from which mud is, he had made from nothing. And if he had made heaven itself and earth, that is the world and all things which are in it, from some matter, as it is written: who made the world from unseen matter, or even formless, as some copies have it, in no way is it to be believed that that very matter, from which the world was made, although formless, although unseen, in whatever way it was, could have existed through itself as coeternal and coeval with God; but whatever its own mode, which it had, so that in some way it might exist and might be able to receive the forms of distinct things, it did not have except from almighty God, by whose benefit a thing exists not only whatever is formed, but also whatever is formable. But between formed and formable this is the difference, that the formed has already received form, but the formable can receive it. But he who supplies form to things, he himself also supplies the ability to be formed, since from him and in him is the most beautiful unchangeable form of all things, and therefore he himself is the one who attributes to any thing not only that it may be beautiful, but also that it may be able to be beautiful. Wherefore it is most rightly believed that God made all things from nothing: because even if the world was made from some matter, that same matter was made from nothing, so that by the most ordered gift of God the first capacity of forms might come to be, and then whatever things have been formed were formed. But we have said this, lest anyone think that the statements of the divine scriptures are contrary to one another, since it is written both that God made all things from nothing and that the world was made from formless matter.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'almighty' for omnipotens, not 'all-powerful'.
Keeps the craftsman imagery of fabricare that Augustine is criticizing; 'builder' would also work but 'maker' preserves the parallel with 'made'.
Standard literal rendering of the phrase; keeps the philosophical force of the argument.
Literal rendering of the Old Latin phrase Augustine quotes; 'invisible' would be more polished but 'unseen' keeps the source wording closer.
Keeps the superlative and the philosophical term 'species' as 'form' to match the formed/formable distinction in the passage.
Literal rendering of the philosophical phrase; 'capacity' preserves the idea of receptivity to form.

bible_refs.note: qui fecisti mundum ex materia inuisa

pass_b_english: Some people have tried to persuade others that God the Father is not almighty. They have not dared to say this outright, but their own traditions show that this is what they think and believe. When they say there is a nature that almighty God did not create, and that he used it to build this world—which they admit is beautifully ordered—they deny that God is almighty. They do not believe he could have made the world unless he used some other nature that already existed and that he himself had not made. They are following the habit of seeing carpenters, house builders, and other workmen, who cannot complete their work unless they are helped by material already prepared. In the same way, they think the maker of the world could not be almighty if he could not build the world unless some nature not made by him helped him as material.

But if they admit that almighty God is the maker of the world, they must confess that he made what he made from nothing. For nothing can exist whose creator he is not, since he is almighty. Even if he made something from something else—as he made the human being from mud—he did not make it from something he himself had not made, because he had made the earth, from which mud comes, from nothing. And if he made heaven and earth itself—that is, the world and everything in it—from some matter, as it is written, "You made the world from unseen matter" (Wisdom of Solomon 11:17), or even from formless matter, as some manuscripts have it, we must in no way believe that this matter from which the world was made—however formless, however unseen, in whatever way it existed—could have existed through itself as coeternal and coeval with God. Whatever mode it had, so that it could exist in some way and receive the forms of distinct things, it had only from almighty God. It is by his gift that a thing exists not only when it is formed, but also when it is formable.

The difference between formed and formable is this: what is formed has already received form, while what is formable can receive it. But the one who gives things form also gives them the very possibility of being formed, because from him and in him is the most beautiful unchangeable form of all things. Therefore he alone is the one who gives to any thing not only that it is beautiful, but also that it can be beautiful. For this reason it is most rightly believed that God made all things from nothing. Even if the world was made from some matter, that matter itself was made from nothing, so that by God's most ordered gift there first came to be the capacity of forms, and then whatever was formed was formed. We have said this so that no one thinks the statements of the divine Scriptures contradict each other, since it is written both that God made all things from nothing and that the world was made from formless matter.

last_rejected.quote: "You made the world from unseen matter" (Wisdom of Solomon 11:17)
last_rejected.source_quote: qui fecisti mundum ex materia inuisa
last_rejected.why: The Latin 'ex materia inuisa' matches Wisdom 11:17 in the Old Latin, but the standard verse reads 'from undetectable matter,' not 'unseen.'
last_rejected.fix: "You made the world from unseen matter" (Wisdom 11:17)
last_rejected.ruling: 'Unseen' is normal range for 'inuisa' (invisible/unseen); 'undetectable' is translator's preference, not error.

last_rejected.quote: They do not believe he could have made the world unless he used some other nature that already existed and that he himself had not made
last_rejected.source_quote: ita omnipotentem deum negant, ut non eum credant mundum potuisse facere, nisi ad eum fabricandum alia natura, quae iam fuerat et quam ipse non fecerat, uteretur
last_rejected.why: English inverts the logic: source says 'they deny God is almighty, so that they do not believe...' (result), not 'they do not believe... unless' (condition).
last_rejected.fix: They deny God is almighty, so that they do not believe he could have made the world unless he used some other nature...
last_rejected.ruling: 'ut non eum credant...nisi...uteretur' rendered as 'do not believe...unless he used' preserves the nisi condition correctly

last_rejected.quote: The difference between formed and formable is this: what is formed has already received form, while what is formable can receive it
last_rejected.source_quote: inter formatum autem et formabile hoc interest, quod formatum iam accepit formam, formabile autem potest accipere
last_rejected.why: English adds 'The difference... is this' frame; source simply states 'between formed and formable this is the difference, that...'
last_rejected.fix: Between formed and formable, this is the difference: what is formed has already received form, while what is formable can receive it
last_rejected.ruling: 'hoc interest, quod' = 'this is the difference, that'; English 'The difference...is this' is equivalent, not a mistranslation
